title: Plan for the outage before it happens: keep meetings and calls running when cloud goes down
summary: Plan for the outage before it happens: keep meetings and calls running when cloud goes down
body_markdown:
When the tools we rely on become unavailable or disrupted, the pain lands on real people. A clinician waits to join a consult. A trader can't reach a client. A small business owner can't confirm tomorrow's orders. An IT admin fields a hundred "is it just me?" messages while the engineers behind the scenes skip dinner to get everything back online. That's what the latest Microsoft 365 and other similar outages looked like for a lot of people. No provider is immune to disruptions, which is exactly why having a plan matters.


Outages like this point to something IT leaders already know: cloud communications depend on a chain of connections, from your office network to your internet provider to the cloud where the services are hosted. A break anywhere in that chain can disrupt work, sometimes even while the service itself is healthy. You can't prevent every break, but you can reduce the impact of many common failures by preparing before one happens.

## Why an SLA won't cover every outage


Many meeting and phone providers offer uptime SLAs in the range of 99.99% or 99.999%. Those SLAs apply to the provider's own infrastructure. They don't cover the internet line into your office going dark, a network problem somewhere between your building and the cloud, or another service provider's bad day spilling over into the tools you use. And when the provider or the cloud is the problem, an SLA credit may arrive weeks later; it doesn't get your meeting back today.


For enterprises, and for organizations in finance, healthcare, government, and other regulated industries, that gap can mean missed appointments, stalled transactions, and compliance challenges on top of a stressful day.


## What keeps running when the connection breaks


This is where Zoom Node comes in.[Zoom Node](https://www.zoom.com/en/products/zoom-node/) is a hybrid business continuity platform that allows you to run core collaboration services on servers in your data center or private cloud while Zoom manages and updates them remotely. Two Zoom Node service modules address common continuity needs: keeping meetings running and keeping phones ringing.


### Meeting Survivability: Help keep your meetings running


Meeting Survivability is a functionality of the[Zoom Meetings Hybrid](https://library.zoom.com/advanced-enterprise-services/zoom-node/zoom-meetings-hybrid) (ZMH) module. When your internet connection or cloud service fails, ZMH is designed to keep most core meeting features available for people on your local network. They can still schedule, join, host, and invite colleagues to meetings. They can also join meetings scheduled earlier, as long as their calendars are available. While IT works on the problem, a bulletin board inside the Zoom app lets admins post updates and share pre-registered meetings, like war rooms, without depending on email or chat, which may also be unavailable during some disruptions.†


### Zoom Phone Local Survivability: Help keep your phone available


[Zoom Phone Local Survivability (ZPLS)](https://library.zoom.com/advanced-enterprise-services/zoom-node/zoom-phone-local-survivability) helps you keep essential calling available when a site loses Internet or its link to the Zoom cloud. Supported phones and Zoom desktop apps register with a local appliance automatically. Failover typically takes about three minutes. After connectivity returns, devices move back to the cloud, and without requiring a manual restart.‡


During an outage, ZPLS lets members of your organization keep calling one another, and even transfer, park, and make conference calls. Calls to and from the outside world can remain available too, provided a survivability session border controller is in place. Admins can set up call forwarding for Zoom-provided numbers ahead of time and assign each site an emergency location identifier, so emergency calls can carry a valid callback number.‡


Both the phone and meeting survivability solutions are robust business continuity tools providing core functionality and supporting most, but not all features available through regular Zoom phone service or Zoom Workplace. Their purpose is to help keep the conversations and collaboration that matter most going until things are back to normal.


## What can remain available during an outage


With Zoom Node and both modules set up ahead of time, here's what you can expect people on your local network will still be able to do in supported scenarios:


- **Meetings:** schedule, join, host, and invite colleagues, plus join meetings scheduled earlier if calendars are available.†
- **Updates from IT:** see admin posts and pre-registered war room meetings on the bulletin board in the Zoom app.†
- **Internal calls:** call colleagues, and transfer, park, and conference calls.‡
- **Outside calls:** make and receive them, with a survivability session border controller in place.‡
- **Emergency calls:** place them with a valid callback number.


## Set up the service and run the drill before the real outage


Survivability features need to be set up before an outage to function as intended. Admins must install the Zoom Node infrastructure and set up Meeting Survivability and Zoom Phone Local Survivability ahead of time. These services are more effective when you've also trained employees, written down your emergency procedures, and agreed on how people will hear from IT.


Zoom provides setup guides, a testing mode, and simulated failover steps, so your team can rehearse on a quiet Tuesday instead of figuring it out mid-outage. When an outage does hit, employees already know your business continuity procedures, and IT can focus on fixing the problem instead of inventing a workaround on the fly.
